narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 54.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Even though you earned a strong undergraduate GPA of 3.8—well above the 3.23 average of accepted students—the model determined that your low decile rankings in both early and later law school years outweighed that positive signal and pulled the outcome toward rejection. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor and worked in your favor, pulling the prediction back toward passing, but not enough to overcome the ranking concerns.

Your LSAT score of 37 was almost exactly average for accepted students and had little influence either way. Your family income, full-time status, gender, and race were not factors in the decision.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your class standing in future semesters, as consistent academic performance in law school appears to be the factor the model trusts most when forecasting bar exam success. Consider seeking academic support or tutoring early to move out of the bottom decile. Once your rankings improve, reapply—your strong GPA already shows you have the ability to succeed.
